clue.text: Earth's grief

parts.note: surface reading: the sorrow of the whole planet; setter's reading: the answer itself is an instruction, its first word telling you to rearrange its second word into Earth

explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: break up the letters of HEART and you get EARTH, so a BROKEN HEART is Earth's, and it also means grief.
explanation.definitionFit: Heartbreak is the common idiom for deep sorrow, especially after losing someone loved.

clue.text: How you don't want your business to go, and what might save you just in time? You betcha

definitions.text: How you don't want your business to go

parts.words: what might save you just in time
parts.note: a boxer can be saved by the bell
an informal yes

explanation.surface: Advice on avoiding a business failure with a last-minute rescue.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm that goes belly-up collapses or goes bankrupt, the idiom from a dead fish floating.

clue.text: Newspaper article with idiot burying the lead

indicators.note: burying puts something underneath, and in journalism the lede is the opening, so the first letter is sent to the bottom

parts.note: a dope is an idiot

explanation.surface: A news story by a fool who hid the most important fact.
explanation.walkthrough: Burying the lead means moving the first letter down to the end. Journalists spell a story's opening 'lede'.
explanation.definitionFit: An op-ed is an opinion piece printed opposite a newspaper's editorial page.

clue.text: John, the Spanish heavyweight

parts.note: el is Spanish for the
a ton is a heavy weight

explanation.surface: A big man named John from Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: Elton John is the British singer, so his first name is clued by his surname.

clue.text: Cheer up sodden drunk? That's tough

parts.note: rah is a cheer

indicators.note: someone drunk staggers about, so the letters are reeling

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Trying to cheer up a soaked drunk is hard going.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard-nosed describes someone tough-minded and unsentimental.

clue.text: Pace wildly around front of card table? OK

indicators.note: around puts the jumbled letters on either side of another piece
front of takes only the opening letter of the next word
doing something wildly means without order, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
first letter of card
taken as written

explanation.surface: Walking frantically round a card table, asking if that's all right.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled letters wrap around C, then TABLE follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Acceptable means satisfactory or good enough, the sense of OK.

clue.text: Diminished bureaucracy had the last word on top

indicators.text: had the last word on top
indicators.note: in a down entry the top is the start, so the closing part of the phrase moves up to lead

parts.note: red tape is bureaucratic procedure

explanation.surface: Cut-back bureaucracy got the final say.
explanation.walkthrough: Red tape is official bureaucratic procedure; the phrase is two words, and the second is moved in front of the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Tapered means narrowed or reduced gradually, so diminished.

clue.text: Filed letters multiple times… as if I care!

parts.note: surface reading: correspondence put away again and again; setter's reading: the letters of the word filed, some used several times, spell the answer

explanation.walkthrough: Only F, I, L, E and D appear, with D and E repeated, so the answer is built of filed's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiddle-dee-dee is an old-fashioned exclamation of dismissive impatience, like whatever.

clue.text: Placard includes caustic synthetic

indicators.note: something that includes another holds it inside itself, so one word wraps round the other

parts.note: a placard is a poster
lye is a caustic alkali

explanation.surface: A protest sign that contains some corrosive artificial material.
explanation.walkthrough: Lye is the old name for sodium hydroxide, a strong alkali used in soap-making.
explanation.definitionFit: Polyester is a man-made fabric, so as a noun it is a synthetic.

clue.text: Decomposing deposit before blowing a whistle, say?

parts.note: to put something is to deposit it
a referee blows the whistle, a ref action

explanation.surface: Something placed down rots before someone blows the whistle on it.
explanation.walkthrough: Before places PUT first. 'Say' flags that blowing a whistle is one example of a ref's action.
explanation.definitionFit: Putrefaction is rotting, the process of organic matter decomposing.

clue.text: Resort island's cold, endless month

indicators.note: something without an end has had its final letter cut off

parts.note: C is the usual abbreviation for cold, as on taps
a month of the year

explanation.surface: A holiday island is chilly for most of one month of the year.
explanation.definitionFit: Capri is an island in the Bay of Naples long famous as a holiday resort.

clue.text: Playthings held back by noisy otters

the letters are held within the run of words that follows, spanning a word break

parts.note: the end of noisy and the start of otters

explanation.surface: Toys being clutched by a family of loud otters.
explanation.definitionFit: Toys are things children play with, which is exactly what playthings are.

clue.text: Dull spin I livened up inside, probably voting Democratic?

indicators.note: inside places the jumbled letters within the phrase that follows
livening something up shakes it into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: the letters of spin and I, rearranged
in US politics red stands for Republican, so a Democratic voter is likely un-red

explanation.surface: A boring spin doctor's line was perked up, perhaps by someone on the left.
explanation.walkthrough: US election maps colour Republican states red and Democratic ones blue, so a Democratic voter is plausibly not red.
explanation.definitionFit: Something uninspired lacks imagination or spark, which makes it dull and flat.

clue.text: Lacking a raise, keep an eye on rosy present-day panacea

lacking means without, so one letter A is dropped

parts.note: to guard is to keep watch over
rosy is red-coloured
now is the present

explanation.surface: Without a pay rise, watching for an optimistic modern cure-all.
explanation.definitionFit: A wonder drug is a medicine hailed as curing everything, which is what a panacea is.

clue.text: Staff hosts replacing 100 with a ruse

a ploy is a ruse or trick

explanation.surface: The workers at a venue host events, swapping a hundred for a trick.
explanation.walkthrough: Take EMCEES and swap its C for PLOY.
explanation.definitionFit: Employees are the people working for an organisation, collectively its staff.

clue.text: Go "om nom nom nom nom" and go "om nom nom nom"—that's what 26 do

parts.words: Go "om nom nom nom nom" and go "om nom nom nom"
parts.note: surface reading: making greedy eating noises over and over; setter's reading: the eating noises frame the answer as eat, a nom, then eat again

explanation.walkthrough: Om nom nom is internet-speak for munching. Split differently, the answer reads EAT NOM EAT, the munching noise sandwiched between two eatings.
explanation.definitionFit: Refusing all flesh is what vegetarians (26 Across) do.

clue.text: Also note Breton

parts.note: and adds one more thing, like also
re is the second note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A further remark in the Breton language.
explanation.walkthrough: Breton looks like an adjective for Brittany, but it is the surname of the French surrealist André Breton.
explanation.definitionFit: André Breton, founder of Surrealism, so his first name is clued by his surname.

clue.text: Shaped cedar, making a bow

indicators.note: shaped means formed into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Cedar wood bent into a bow, as for archery.
explanation.definitionFit: Arced means curved in an arch, the shape of a bow.

clue.text: Playwright to mark box on a list for audience

parts.words: to mark box on a list
parts.note: ticking a box on a list is checking it off

explanation.definitionFit: Anton Chekhov was the Russian dramatist who wrote The Seagull and The Cherry Orchard.

clue.text: Validate corrupt ex-president within natural disaster

taken as written
